last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 8 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}8 & 7 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 17
?

Let B={[32],[23]} and C={[1−1],[1−2]} be bases of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

a
[−8−755]
b
[7558]
c
[8−5−57]
d
[78−5−5]
e
[87−5−5]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[1132−1−223]R2:=R2+R1∼[11320−155]R2:=(−1)R2∼[113201−5−5]R1:=R1+(−1)R2∼[108701−5−5]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C. Therefore, we have PB→C=[87−5−5].
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases

solution.reasoning: The columns are the C-coordinates of the B basis vectors. Since 8c_1-5c_2=(3,2)^T and 7c_1-5c_2=(2,3)^T, the matrix is [[8,7],[-5,-5]], matching option e. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the example supports only the method.

feedback.name: Question 17
feedback.problem: Let $B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\}$ and $C=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 8 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}8 & 7 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}].
$$

Let B={[32],[23]} and C={[1−1],[1−2]} be bases of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

a
[−8−755]
b
[7558]
c
[8−5−57]
d
[78−5−5]

[87−5−5]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[1132−1−223]R2:=R2+R1∼[11320−155]R2:=(−1)R2∼[113201−5−5]R1:=R1+(−1)R2∼[108701−5−5]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C. Therefore, we have PB→C=[87−5−5].

question.name: Question 18
question.problem: Let $B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 11\end{aligned}]\}$ and $C=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 18
?

Let B={[15],[211]} and C={[13],[02]} be bases of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B.

a
[3−1−21]
b
[232−2]
c
[−2−232]
d
[3−42−2]
e
[5−4−22]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of C relative to the basis B.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of c1 and c2 relative to the basis B. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||b1b2c1c2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[121051132]R2:=R2+(−5)R1∼[121001−22]R1:=R1+(−2)R2∼[105−401−22]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B. Therefore, we have PC→B=[5−4−22].
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases

solution.reasoning: The columns are the B-coordinates of c_1 and c_2. Since 5b_1-2b_2=(1,3)^T=c_1 and -4b_1+2b_2=(0,2)^T=c_2, the matrix is [[5,-4],[-2,2]], matching option e. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the example supports only the method.

feedback.name: Question 18
feedback.problem: Let $B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 11\end{aligned}]\}$ and $C=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $C$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 11 & 3 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

question.problem: Let $B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\}$  be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{e}_{1},{e}_{2}\}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & -6 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

last_observation.name: Question 19
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{e}_{1},{e}_{2}\}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & -6 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

question.html:
Question 19
?

Let B={[13],[−3−6]} be a basis of R2 and let S be the standard basis of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B.

a
[1−2−113]
b
[1−213−1]
c
[−21−13]
d
[−11−213]
e
[−21−113]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and S as {b1,b2} and {e1,e2}, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of R2 consists of the vectors e1=[10],e2=[01].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of S relative to the basis B.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of e1 and e2 relative to the basis B. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||b1b2e1e2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[1−3103−601]R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[1−31003−31]R2:=13R2∼[1−31001−113]R1:=R1+3R2∼[10−2101−113]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B. Therefore, we have PS→B=[−21−113]
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases

solution.reasoning: The matrix from B to S has the basis vectors as columns: [[1,-3],[3,-6]]. Its determinant is -6+9=3, so its inverse, the matrix from S to B, is (1/3)[[-6,3],[-3,1]]=[[-2,1],[-1,1/3]], matching option e. feedback.name: Question 19
feedback.problem: Let $B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\}$  be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{e}_{1},{e}_{2}\}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & -6 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

a

Let's denote the vectors of B and S as {b1,b2} and {e1,e2}, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of R2 consists of the vectors e1=[10],e2=[01].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of S relative to the basis B.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of e1 and e2 relative to the basis B. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||b1b2e1e2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[1−3103−601]R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[1−31003−31]R2:=13R2∼[1−31001−113]R1:=R1+3R2∼[10−2101−113]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B. Therefore, we have PS→B=[−21−113]

question.name: Question 20
question.problem: Let $B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\}$ and $C=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 9 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 20
?

Let B={[39],[66]} and C={[13],[23]} be bases of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

a
[3−204]
b
[2204]
c
[−2104]
d
[2004]
e
[3012]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[12363396]R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[12360−30−12]R2:=−13R2∼[12360104]R1:=R1+(−2)R2∼[103−20104]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C. Therefore, we have PB→C=[3−204].

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 9 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 20
?

Let B={[39],[66]} and C={[13],[23]} be bases of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

a
[3−204]
b
[2204]
c
[−2104]
d
[2004]
e
[3012]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[12363396]R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[12360−30−12]R2:=−13R2∼[12360104]R1:=R1+(−2)R2∼[103−20104]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C. Therefore, we have PB→C=[3−204].
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases

solution.reasoning: The columns are the C-coordinates of the B basis vectors. Since b_1=3c_1 and b_2=-2c_1+4c_2, the matrix is [[3,-2],[0,4]], matching option a. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the example supports only the method.

feedback.name: Question 20
feedback.problem: Let $B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\}$ and $C=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\}$ be bases of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 9 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Question 20
?

Let B={[39],[66]} and C={[13],[23]} be bases of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

a
[3−204]
b
[2204]
c
[−2104]
d
[2004]
e
[3012]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[12363396]R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[12360−30−12]R2:=−13R2∼[12360104]R1:=R1+(−2)R2∼[103−20104]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C. Therefore, we have PB→C=[3−204].

tutorial.problem:
Given two bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ of a vector space $V,$ the **change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$** is the matrix $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$.

In expanded form, the matrix looks as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/a915359feeb5fa10688429f0925ab07ec3767d001a2b0b5f13a5914a606b8236.svg)

For example, let's consider two bases $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ given by 

$$
\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2\}, \qquad\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2\}.
$$

If we happen to know that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/8482b6adf4b524a5ac35b1a6739a7b8971b7dfc0f54df7246c314dcbc38dcb45.svg) 

then the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}= & [\begin{aligned}-12 & 3 \\ 11 & 6\end{aligned}]. \\  & \,{↑}_{[{b}_{1}]_{C}}\,{↑}_{[{b}_{2}]_{C}}\end{aligned}
$$

The beauty of the change-of-coordinates matrix is that it allows us to express the vector $[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}$ in the basis $\mathcal C$ via the transformation

$$
[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal C} = P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} \cdot [\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}.
$$

This can be visualized as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/ede6eb17f0667a8974902bf2d181150eeb3c665faa3059bb818bb9a61b631511.png)

tutorial.content:
Given two bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ of a vector space $V,$ the **change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$** is the matrix $P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}},$ whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$.

In expanded form, the matrix looks as follows:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/a915359feeb5fa10688429f0925ab07ec3767d001a2b0b5f13a5914a606b8236.svg)

For example, let's consider two bases $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ given by 

$$
\mathcal{B}=\{\mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2\}, \qquad\mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2\}.
$$

If we happen to know that

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/8482b6adf4b524a5ac35b1a6739a7b8971b7dfc0f54df7246c314dcbc38dcb45.svg) 

then the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}= & [\begin{aligned}-12 & 3 \\ 11 & 6\end{aligned}]. \\  & \,{↑}_{[{b}_{1}]_{C}}\,{↑}_{[{b}_{2}]_{C}}\end{aligned}
$$

The beauty of the change-of-coordinates matrix is that it allows us to express the vector $[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}$ in the basis $\mathcal C$ via the transformation

$$
[\mathbf x]_{\mathcal C} = P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} \cdot [\mathbf x]_{\mathcal B}.
$$

This can be visualized as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/ede6eb17f0667a8974902bf2d181150eeb3c665faa3059bb818bb9a61b631511.png)

steps.name: Question 1
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Given a Linear Connection Between Two Bases
steps.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -7\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -7 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

question.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -7\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -7 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Let B={b1,b2} and C={c1,c2} be bases of R2. If b1=2c1−7c2 and b2=4c2−3c1, find the change-of-coordinates matrix PB→C from B to C.

a
[24−7−3]
b
[42−3−7]
c
[−324−7]
d
[2−3−74]
e
[42−7−3]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The coordinates of the vectors in B relative to the basis C are

[b1]C=[2−7],[b2]C=[−34].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Therefore, we obtain

PB→C=[2−3−74].
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Given a Linear Connection Between Two Bases

steps.name: Question 2
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Given a Linear Connection Between Two Bases
steps.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=2,$ $b=2,$ and $c=5.$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}\}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}.$ 
What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={c}_{1}+2{c}_{2}-{c}_{3}, \\ {b}_{2} & =5{c}_{3}+2{c}_{2}, \\ {b}_{3} & ={c}_{2}-{c}_{1},\end{aligned}
$$

and  the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ a & b & 1 \\ -1 & c & 0\end{aligned}]?
$$
question.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=2,$ $b=2,$ and $c=5.$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Let B={b1,b2,b3} and C={c1,c2,c3} be bases of R3. What are the values of a,b, and c if

b1=c1+2c2−c3,b2=5c3+2c2,b3=c2−c1,

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is

PB→C=[10−1ab1−1c0]?

a
a=1, b=−2, and c=5
b
a=0, b=2, and c=−1
c
a=1, b=2, and c=0
d
a=2, b=0, and c=−1
e
a=2, b=2, and c=5
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The coordinates of the vectors in B relative to the basis C are

[b1]C=[12−1],[b2]C=[025],[b3]C=[−110].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Therefore, we obtain

PB→C=[10−1221−150].

Finally, a=2, b=2, and c=5.

question.html:
Question 4
?

Let B={b1,b2} and C={c1,c2} be bases of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix PB→C from B to C given that

[b1]C=[1−2],[b2]C=[−13].

a
[2−1−13]
b
[2−3−11]
c
[1−1−23]
d
[1−1−32]
e
[3−1−21]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Therefore, we obtain

PB→C=[1−1−23].
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Given a Linear Connection Between Two Bases

steps.name: Question 5
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Given a Linear Connection Between Two Bases
steps.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=1,$ $b=0,$ and $c=-1.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ and $C=\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}\}$ be bases of ${R}^{3}.$ 
What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{1} & ={c}_{1}+{c}_{2}-{c}_{3}, \\ {b}_{2} & =2{c}_{3}+{c}_{2}, \\ {b}_{3} & =-{c}_{3}+2{c}_{1},\end{aligned}
$$

and  the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & a & b \\ -1 & 2 & c\end{aligned}]?
$$
question.worked_solution:
The coordinates of the vectors in $B$ relative to the basis $C$ are

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=1,$ $b=0,$ and $c=-1.$

Question 5
?

Let B={b1,b2,b3} and C={c1,c2,c3} be bases of R3. What are the values of a,b, and c if

b1=c1+c2−c3,b2=2c3+c2,b3=−c3+2c1,

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is

PB→C=[1021ab−12c]?

a
a=0, b=1, and c=−1
b
a=1, b=0, and c=−1
c
a=−1, b=0, and c=−1
d
a=1, b=1, and c=0
e
a=0, b=−1, and c=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The coordinates of the vectors in B relative to the basis C are

[b1]C=[11−1],[b2]C=[012],[b3]C=[20−1].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Therefore, we obtain

PB→C=[102110−12−1].

Finally, a=1, b=0, and c=−1.

steps.name: Question 6
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
steps.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors of $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ 
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{B\to S}$ from $B$ to $S$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2},$ given by

$$

$$

$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}].

question.html:
Question 6
?

Let B={b1,b2} be a basis of R2 and let S be the standard basis of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix PB→S from B to S if b1=[1−2],b2=[1−3].

a
[−211−3]
b
[11−2−3]
c
[−2−311]
d
[11−3−2]
e
[−3121]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the standard basis of R2 consists of the vectors e1 and e2, given by e1=[10],e2=[01].

The components of the vectors of B are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

[b1]S=[1−2],[b2]S=[1−3]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis S.

Therefore, we obtain PB→S=[11−2−3].
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis

steps.name: Question 7
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
steps.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -5 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=-3,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=1.$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}a & -5 & 0 \\ 4 & b & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & c\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -5 & 0 \\ 4 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=-3,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=1.$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Let B={b1,b2,b3} be a basis of R3 and let S be the standard basis of R3. What are the values of a,b, and c if

b1=[−340],b2=[−5−10],b3=[001],

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is

PB→S=[a−504b000c].

a
a=−3, b=0, and c=4
b
a=−3, b=−1, and c=1
c
a=0, b=0, and c=1
d
a=−3, b=0, and c=0
e
a=−5, b=4, and c=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the standard basis of R3 consists of the vectors e1,e2, and e3, given by e1=[100],e2=[010],e3=[001].

The components of the vectors in B are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

[b1]S=[−340],[b2]S=[−5−10],[b3]S=[001]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis S.

Therefore, we obtain PB→S=[−3−504−10001].

Finally, a=−3, b=−1, and c=1.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis

steps.name: Question 8
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
steps.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & -1 \\ -4 & 1 & 2 \\ 7 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=0,$ $b=2,$ and $c=5.$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}a & 3 & -1 \\ -4 & 1 & b \\ 7 & c & 0\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 3 & -1 \\ -4 & 1 & 2 \\ 7 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=0,$ $b=2,$ and $c=5.$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Let B={b1,b2,b3} be a basis of R3 and let S be the standard basis of R3. What are the values of a,b, and c if

b1=[0−47],b2=[315],b3=[−120],

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is

PB→S=[a3−1−41b7c0].

a
a=7, b=2, and c=3.
b
a=−1, b=−4, and c=2.
c
a=0, b=5, and c=2.
d
a=7, b=3, and c=2.
e
a=0, b=2, and c=5.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the standard basis of R3 consists of the vectors e1,e2, and e3, given by e1=[100],e2=[010],e3=[001].

The components of the vectors in B are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

[b1]S=[0−47],[b2]S=[315],[b3]S=[−120]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis S.

Therefore, we obtain PB→S=[03−1−412750].

Finally, a=0, b=2, and c=5.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis

steps.name: Question 9
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
steps.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=0,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-5.$

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ be a basis of ${R}^{3}$ and let $S$ be the standard basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What are the values of $a,b,$ and $c$ if 

$$
{b}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,{b}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is 

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & a \\ b & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & c & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & -5 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=0,$ $b=-1,$ and $c=-5.$

question.html:
Question 9
?

Let B={b1,b2,b3} be a basis of R3 and let S be the standard basis of R3. What are the values of a,b, and c if

b1=[2−13],b2=[4−2−5],b3=[032],

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is

PB→S=[24ab−233c2].

a
a=2, b=3, and c=−5
b
a=0, b=−1, and c=−5
c
a=3, b=4, and c=3
d
a=2, b=−1, and c=−2
e
a=3, b=−2, and c=4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the standard basis of R3 consists of the vectors e1,e2, and e3, given by e1=[100],e2=[010],e3=[001].

The components of the vectors in B are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

[b1]S=[2−13],[b2]S=[4−2−5],[b3]S=[032]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to S is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis S.

Therefore, we obtain PB→S=[240−1−233−52].

Finally, a=0, b=−1, and c=−5.

steps.name: Question 10
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix When One of the Bases is the Standard Basis
steps.worked_solution:
Recall  that the standard basis of ${R}^{3}$ consists of the vectors ${e}_{1},{e}_{2},$ and ${e}_{3},$ given by

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The components of the vectors in $B$ are just the coordinates relative to the standard basis:

$$
[{b}_{1}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{2}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 0 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,[{b}_{3}]_{S}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is a matrix whose respective columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $S.$ 

Therefore, we obtain

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -8 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 5 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $a=-2,$ $b=0,$ and $c=-3.$

tutorial.name: The Inverse of a Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
tutorial.problem:
Since the columns of a change-of-coordinates matrix are linearly independent, the matrix must be invertible.

In fact, the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ to $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ are the inverses of each other:

$$
P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}
	\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
	P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}.
$$

Question 12

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis B to the basis C is given by PB→C=[2−3−35]., Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B .

a
[3352]
b
[52−3−3]
c
[5−3−32]
d
[3253]
e
[5332]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C. Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of PB→C, we get

PC→B=PB→C−1=[2−3−35]−1=12⋅5−(−3)⋅(−3)[5332]=1⋅[5332]=[5332].
question.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix

steps.name: Question 13
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
steps.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-1)-(-2)\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -1 \\ \frac{1}{2} & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$
question.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-1)-(-2)\cdot 1}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2})\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & -1 \\ \frac{1}{2} & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis C to the basis B is given by PC→B=[4−21−1]. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

a
[1−112−2]
b
[12−112−2]
c
[1−1212−2]
d
[−1−12−2−1]
e
[−1−1212−2]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B. Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of PC→B, we get PB→C=PC→B−1=[4−21−1]−1=14⋅(−1)−(−2)⋅1[−12−14]=(−12)⋅[−12−14]=[12−112−2].
question.knowledge_point: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix

steps.name: Question 14
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
steps.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{7\cdot 4-3\cdot 9}[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 14
question.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $C$ to the basis $B$ is given by
${P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}].$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$  .
question.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C} & ={P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}7 & 3 \\ 9 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{7\cdot 4-3\cdot 9}[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ -9 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis C to the basis B is given by PC→B=[7394]. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C .

a
[9−7−43]
b
[4397]
c
[4−3−97]
d
[4−9−37]
e
[7−3−94]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B. Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of PC→B, we get

PB→C=PC→B−1=[7394]−1=17⋅4−3⋅9[4−3−97]=1⋅[4−3−97]=[4−3−97].

steps.name: Question 15
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Using the Invertibility Property of the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix
steps.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $B$ to the basis $C$ is given by 
${P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].$
Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$  .
question.worked_solution:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B$ is the inverse of the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we simply need to find the inverse of the given matrix.

Computing the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B} & ={P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-3)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =1\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorial.name: Computing the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Using Row-Reduction
tutorial.problem:
Suppose that we have bases $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \},$ and we want to find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C},$ denoted $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}.$

Recall that the columns of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C},$ that is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/ccc08d16a25b48a7e5526027f6e5d9f7f9fe093ae7918693eba290a2b0b02746.svg)

To compute $P_{\small{\color{black}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{black}\mathcal{C}}},$ we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/ffbf7bcec60305d191d31a64d3caf9a5623e74419150082948833199ca57fa89.svg)

If we reduce the left-hand side of $M$ to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination, $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ will emerge on the right-hand side:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/1fd32bdb4a391ee5867f541573b961491107000372308b6c836a0bfbe4b339c7.svg)

tutorial.content:
Suppose that we have bases $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\mathcal{C}=\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \},$ and we want to find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C},$ denoted $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}.$

Recall that the columns of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C},$ that is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/ccc08d16a25b48a7e5526027f6e5d9f7f9fe093ae7918693eba290a2b0b02746.svg)

To compute $P_{\small{\color{black}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{black}\mathcal{C}}},$ we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/ffbf7bcec60305d191d31a64d3caf9a5623e74419150082948833199ca57fa89.svg)

If we reduce the left-hand side of $M$ to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination, $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ will emerge on the right-hand side:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/1fd32bdb4a391ee5867f541573b961491107000372308b6c836a0bfbe4b339c7.svg)

steps.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \},$ respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

So, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14275083/assets/b0a97c1405b8f3399deb1316be49b035a9f2efa9beeadd5b1af2b372514ade10.svg)

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -5 & 7 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 13\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & 22 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 13\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}= & [\begin{aligned}\,4 & 22 \\ \,1 & 13\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

steps.name: Question 16
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
steps.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{e}_{1},{e}_{2}\}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

question.name: Question 16
question.problem: Let $B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$  be a basis of ${R}^{2}$ and $S$ is the standard basis of ${R}^{2}.$ Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$
question.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{e}_{1},{e}_{2}\}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Let B={[12],[11]} be a basis of R2 and S is the standard basis of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B.

EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and S as {b1,b2} and {e1,e2}, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of R2 consists of the vectors e1=[10],e2=[01].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of S relative to the basis B.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of e1 and e2 relative to the basis B. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||b1b2e1e2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: M=[11102101]R2:=R2+(−2)R1∼[11100−1−21]R2:=(−1)R2∼[1110012−1]R1:=R1+(−1)R2∼[10−11012−1]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B. Therefore, we have PS→B=[−112−1].

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ -1 & -2 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -5\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 8 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 & -5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}8 & 7 \\ -5 & -5\end{aligned}].

Let B={[15],[211]} and C={[13],[02]} be bases of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B.

a
[3−1−21]
b
[232−2]

[−2−232]

[5−4−22]

EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of C relative to the basis B.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of c1 and c2 relative to the basis B. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||b1b2c1c2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[121051132]R2:=R2+(−5)R1∼[121001−22]R1:=R1+(−2)R2∼[105−401−22]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from C to B. Therefore, we have PC→B=[5−4−22].

steps.name: Question 19
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
steps.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $S$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{e}_{1},{e}_{2}\}$, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of ${R}^{2}$ consists of the vectors

$$
{e}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{e}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $S$ relative to the basis $B.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${e}_{1}$ and ${e}_{2}$ relative to the basis $B.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} & {e}_{1} & {e}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 3 & -6 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $S$ to $B.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{S\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & \frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 19
?

Let B={[13],[−3−6]} be a basis of R2 and let S be the standard basis of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B.

a
[1−2−113]
b
[1−213−1]
c
[−21−13]
d
[−11−213]
e
[−21−113]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and S as {b1,b2} and {e1,e2}, respectively. Recall that the standard basis of R2 consists of the vectors e1=[10],e2=[01].

The change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of S relative to the basis B.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of e1 and e2 relative to the basis B. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||b1b2e1e2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[1−3103−601]R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[1−31003−31]R2:=13R2∼[1−31001−113]R1:=R1+3R2∼[10−2101−113]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from S to B. Therefore, we have PS→B=[−21−113]

steps.name: Question 20
steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix Between Two Bases
steps.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 9 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 9 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$ Therefore, we have

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].

question.html:
Question 20
?

Let B={[39],[66]} and C={[13],[23]} be bases of R2. Find the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C.

a
[3−204]
b
[2204]
c
[−2104]
d
[2004]
e
[3012]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's denote the vectors of B and C as {b1,b2} and {c1,c2}, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the vectors of B relative to the basis C.

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of b1 and b2 relative to the basis C. We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix M=[||||c1c2b1b2||||].

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

M=[12363396]R2:=R2+(−3)R1∼[12360−30−12]R2:=−13R2∼[12360104]R1:=R1+(−2)R2∼[103−20104]

On the right-hand side, we obtain the change-of-coordinates matrix from B to C. Therefore, we have PB→C=[3−204].
